caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000678
attempts.paper_title: Hulsey, D., Zumwalt, K., Mazzucato, L., McCormick, D. A., & Jaramillo, S. (2024). Decision-making dynamics are predicted by arousal and uninstructed movements. Cell Reports, 43(1), 113709.
attempts.entry_title: Arousal, uninstructed movements and decision-making states in mice (Hulsey et al. 2024)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Hulsey, Zumwalt, Mazzucato, McCormick and Jaramillo (2024) on dandiset 000678, which holds the stage 5 and 6 behavioral sessions of 13 mice performing auditory or visual discrimination, with pupil diameter, face motion energy and locomotion speed. It fits the paper's GLM-HMM to each mouse's choices, labels the performance states, and relates the states to the arousal and movement measures, including the support vector machine decoding of the states.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Hulsey et al. (2024) from dandiset 000678

outcomes.statement: Of 31 mice, 13 met the inclusion criteria (8 auditory, 5 visual task), with 381 of their 500 stage 5 and 6 sessions included.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Training and inclusion criteria, last paragraph; Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6
outcomes.quote: 13 of 31 mice met inclusion criteria, with a total of 381 of their 500 stage 5 and 6 training sessions included for further analysis
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds 13 mice, 8 on the auditory and 5 on the visual task, each with at least 10 passing sessions. Of its 391 stage 5 and 6 sessions, 376 pass the STAR Methods criteria counted from the reward series and 375 counted from the hits, against 381 in the paper. The sessions failing either count are listed in the notebook; 14 fail both (13 with fewer than 100 rewards, 1 with less than 20% at one port) and 3 fail one count only. The paper's 500 stage 5 and 6 sessions and its 18 excluded mice are not in the dandiset.
deviations: The sessions of every later analysis are the 376 that pass the criteria by the reward count; the paper analysed 381, and the dandiset does not say which.

outcomes.statement: Mice that reached proficiency took 21 +/- 8 training sessions to reach stage 5.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Training and inclusion criteria, last paragraph
outcomes.quote: Mice that reached proficiency took 21 ± 8 training sessions to reach stage 5
outcomes.notes: Every session in the dandiset is stage 5 or 6 (metadata training_stage), so the training sessions before stage 5 cannot be counted. They are not public elsewhere as far as the paper and the dandiset say.

outcomes.statement: In stage 6, responses to distractors of the untrained modality were below 10%, with no discernible change in task performance.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Training and inclusion criteria, Stage 6
outcomes.quote: There was no discernible change in task performance, and response rates to the distractors were <10%
outcomes.notes: Distractor trials have outcome 4 (false alarm, a lick) or 8 (correct reject). Under reading (c), 2,446 of 47,037 stage 6 distractor trials had a lick, 5.2%. Under readings (a) and (b), 7 of the 8 mice with stage 6 sessions are below 10%; BW053 is at 16.2% pooled and 15.3% over sessions. "No discriminable change in performance" is not tested; the fraction correct of responded target trials differs between stages by at most 5.4 points.

outcomes.statement: Cross-validated GLM-HMMs fit separately to each of the 13 mice gave between 3 and 5 states per mouse.
outcomes.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure S2
outcomes.quote: we fit GLM-HMMs separately to each of the 13 mice that reached proficiency on the sensory discrimination task (8 auditory and 5 visual task performers). While there was diversity in the best number of states across subjects (3–5 states
outcomes.notes: With 10 random initialisations per fold, as the paper, both readings of O1 give 3 states in five mice and 4 in eight, inside the claimed 3 to 5 as the criterion requires; no mouse has 5 states, so the largest count is 4 against the paper's 5. The MAP plateau is never larger than the MLE plateau. 38 of the 9,100 cross-validation fits stopped at 1,000 iterations.
deviations: The GLM-HMM of the paper's ssm fork is reimplemented (hulsey.py) with the same model, priors, initialisation scheme, EM updates and stopping rule; its random initial values differ from ssm's. The test log probability includes the log prior, as ssm's log_probability does.

The visual stimulus values follow loadbehavior.get_stim_vals of the paper's code (uobrainflex at ef48985), which for a file with a visual_gabor_angle column maps the difficulty codes 0, 1 and 2 to the session's distinct values of abs(angle - 45) / 45, largest first, and otherwise to 1, 0.8 and 0.6. 118 of the 141 visual-task sessions get 1, 0.6 and 0.2 and the other 23 get 1, 0.8 and 0.6. The first version of this attempt used 1, 0.8 and 0.6 for every session.
Fit on the 376 sessions that pass the inclusion criteria (see cohort-inclusion).

outcomes.statement: For the example mouse, a 4-state GLM-HMM was selected; it predicted 78% of choices against 70% for a one-state model.
outcomes.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 5; Figure 1G
outcomes.quote: A one-state GLM-HMM, equivalent to assuming stationary performance during training, correctly predicted the choice of the example mouse on 70% of trials, while the best-fit 4-state GLM-HMM correctly predicted 78% of choices
outcomes.notes: BW046 gets 4 states under both readings of O1; one-state accuracy 70.2%, 4-state accuracy 78.1%, computed as in fig2d-prediction-accuracy.
deviations: As for figs2-n-states and fig2d-prediction-accuracy.

outcomes.statement: Six stereotyped performance states emerged across mice. Every mouse had an optimal and a disengaged state and at least one sub-optimal state (bias left or right, avoid left or right).
outcomes.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: Each subject exhibited both optimal (state 1) and disengaged (state 2) states, along with at least one additional sub-optimal performance state
outcomes.notes: All 13 mice have an optimal, a disengaged and at least one other state, and each of the 21 other states is matched to a sub-optimal template. Mice per type are bias left 6, avoid right 5, bias right 6 and avoid left 4 (Figure 2A gives 6, 4, 5 and 5; not deciding). Under M3 the other states are matched only to the four sub-optimal templates, so that part of the criterion cannot fail; the distances to all six templates, printed for BW061 and BW048, put each of their states nearest the template of its label. In BW059 one state has no trial with a posterior of at least 0.8 in the sessions where the optimal state occurs, so its psychometric is all missing; Figure2.py's nansum would score it 0 against every template and mislabel the mouse's optimal state. That state (432 trials over all sessions) is typed on all sessions, as avoid right. The question is asked of the paper's authors (findings).
deviations: Assumption. A state with no discrete-state trial in the sessions where the optimal state occurs is typed on all of the mouse's sessions; Figure2.py has no rule for it (it would score the state as equal to every template). Affects one state of BW059.
As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: Mice spent the largest proportion of trials in the optimal state (around half), more than in the disengaged, sub-optimal or indeterminate states; 13.1% +/- 1.6% of trials were indeterminate.
outcomes.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Subjects spent the largest proportion of trials in the optimal performance state ... and only 13.1% ± 1.6% of trials were in an indeterminate state
outcomes.notes: On sessions in which the optimal state occurs, the optimal state holds 50.5% +/- 3.3% of trials, disengaged 12.7%, sub-optimal 23.7% and indeterminate 13.1% +/- 1.6%, within the expected 13.1 +/- 1.6. The optimal share is larger than each other share in 13 of 13 mice (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.00024 for each).
deviations: As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: Epochs of the optimal state lasted longer than disengaged and sub-optimal epochs (about 37 against about 15 trials), and the median transition between discrete states took 3.4 +/- 0.3 trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Discussion, paragraph beginning "Here, we used recently implemented GLM-HMMs"; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Additionally, epochs of the optimal state lasted longer than those of sub-optimal states ... and the median transition time between discrete states (dwell time in indeterminate states) was 3.4 ± 0.3 trials
outcomes.notes: Optimal epochs are longer than disengaged and sub-optimal epochs in 13 of 13 mice under every reading (p = 0.00024). The median indeterminate dwell is 3.31 +/- 0.35 trials, within 3.4 +/- 0.3. The 37 is not matched under any reading. Under reading (a) the optimal dwell is 43.8 trials with the code's dwell (y) and 42.8 as run length (x), above 40.7; the disengaged dwell is 14.0 (13.8), within 15 +/- 1.5, and the sub-optimal 19.1 (18.1), above it. Readings (b) and (c) give optimal dwells of 73.2 to 74.1 and 49.3 to 50.3. The measured values are the indeterminate dwell and the optimal and disengaged dwells under (a) and (y).
deviations: flex_hmm.get_dwell_times adds a last epoch of dwell 0 when a session's last trial differs from the one before it, which also adds a zero indeterminate dwell. The code's output is used, as the claims file reads it; without the 3 such epochs the indeterminate dwell and the medians are unchanged (shown in the notebook).
As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: The best-fit GLM-HMM predicted 75.7% +/- 1.7% of choices, a 10.8% +/- 1.3% improvement over a one-state (static performance) model.
outcomes.source: Results, Mice switch between several performance states, paragraph 6; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: the best-fit GLM-HMM correctly predicted 75.7% ± 1.7% of choices, a significant 10.8% ± 1.3% improvement over the classical static-performance assumption
outcomes.notes: Best model 76.2% +/- 1.6%, one state 65.1% +/- 2.2%, gain 11.0 +/- 1.3 points under reading (a) (17.8% +/- 2.5% relative under (b), outside). Better in 13 of 13 mice, Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.00024 (rank-sum p = 0.00025).
deviations: The paper's code computes the filtered posterior of the preceding test trials by re-running expected_states on each prefix; here one forward pass gives the same filtered probabilities.
As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: The probability of being in the optimal state follows an inverted-U function of pupil diameter, highest at intermediate diameters, in nearly all mice.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 2; Figure 3C; Figure S3
outcomes.quote: The inverted-U relationship was found in nearly all subjects, and the pupil diameter that gave the highest probability for being in the optimal state was calculated for each
outcomes.notes: Reading (i) holds in 13 of 13 mice and reading (ii) in 13 of 13, so "nearly all" holds under (a) and (b). Polynomial degrees 2 to 6 were selected by the elbow rule.
deviations: As Figure3.py, a state absent from a bin with more than 5 trials leaves that bin missing, so a bin with no optimal trial is not a zero; this follows the code.
As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: The optimal pupil diameter is smaller in mice performing the auditory task than in those performing the visual task.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 2; Figure 3D
outcomes.quote: Subjects performing the auditory task had significantly smaller optimal pupil sizes than those performing the visual task
outcomes.notes: Median optimal pupil 0.649 of the session maximum for the 8 auditory mice and 0.739 for the 5 visual mice; Wilcoxon rank-sum p = 0.013 (exact Mann-Whitney p = 0.011; paper 0.008).

outcomes.statement: Across mice, aligned to each mouse's optimal pupil, the probability of the optimal state is an inverted U and the probability of the disengaged state a U of pupil diameter; this holds also on trials when the mice were stationary.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 3; Figure 3E
outcomes.quote: we found a prominent U relationship between the probability of being in the disengaged state and pupil diameter ... These relationships were maintained when considering only trials where the mice were stationary
outcomes.notes: On all trials, over 23 bins with at least 7 mice, the second-order fit to mean P(optimal) has a negative quadratic term (vertex -0.9% from the optimal pupil) and to P(disengaged) a positive one (vertex -1.6%). On stationary trials under reading (b), absolute speed below 0.02 m/s (32,495 trials, 21 bins), both hold (vertices -3.3 and -6.1). Counting the 214 trials at or below -0.02 m/s as stationary, as the first version did, changes the vertices by at most 0.1. Reading (a), speed exactly 0, leaves 1,821 trials and no bin with 7 mice, so it cannot be tested. Exact zeros depend on rounding in the filter (9,869 more trials have a speed below 1e-9 m/s that is not exactly 0), and a run on another machine counted 1,879.
deviations: Stationary under reading (b) is taken as absolute speed below 0.02 m/s, so that backward movement is not counted as stationary.

outcomes.statement: Second-order cross-validated regression fits of optimal-state probability are poorer for face motion energy (r2 0.49 +/- 0.08) and locomotion speed (0.44 +/- 0.07) than for pupil diameter (0.72 +/- 0.03).
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 4; Figure S4
outcomes.quote: pupil diameter: r 2 = 0.72 ± 0.03; face motion energy: r 2 = 0.49 ± 0.08, Wilcoxon signed-rank test vs. pupil: p = 0.04, locomotion speed: r 2 = 0.44 ± 0.07, Wilcoxon signed-rank test vs. pupil: p = 0.002

statistics.about: face motion energy against pupil r2

outcomes.notes: Pupil r2 0.690 +/- 0.039 (within 0.72 +/- 0.03). Face 0.428 +/- 0.092 with plotting bins (a), within, and 0.409 with 50 bins (b), just outside. Locomotion 0.567 (a), outside (0.570 in a run on another machine), and 0.413 (b), within. No bin reading puts all three in tolerance. Both are lower than pupil on average (by 0.12 to 0.28), but by Wilcoxon only locomotion under (b) is lower at p < 0.05 (p = 0.011); face p = 0.11 and 0.057, locomotion (a) p = 0.41. The criterion's r2 comes from one shuffled split per mouse, as 4_optimal_pupils.py; the mean over 10 splits gives pupil 0.682 +/- 0.043 (BW051 from 0.001 to 0.562 over the splits) and the same test results (face p = 0.15 and 0.068, locomotion p = 0.34 and 0.013). The measured values are pupil, face (a) and locomotion (a).
deviations: As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: Optimal-state probability peaks at intermediate values of the movement index, an inverted U similar to pupil diameter (cross-validated r2 0.63 +/- 0.06, not different from pupil).
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5; Figure 3F; Figure S5D
outcomes.quote: Using this combined movement index, a clear inverted-U pattern emerged, showing that optimal performance state occupancy peaked at intermediate levels of uninstructed movement, similar to that of pupil diameter (regression of movement index vs. optimal state, cross-validated r 2 = 0.63 ± 0.06
outcomes.notes: The mean P(optimal) over the 0.25 movement-index bins with at least 7 mice has a negative quadratic term with its vertex at 0.28, inside -4.25 to 3.75. The r2 is 0.574 +/- 0.057 under (a), within 0.63 +/- 0.06 and close to its lower bound, and 0.533 under (b), outside. It does not differ from pupil's (difference -0.12, p = 0.22 under (a); p = 0.17 under (b)). Over 10 shuffled splits per mouse the r2 is 0.573 (a) and 0.522 (b).
deviations: As for figs2-n-states.

outcomes.statement: The probability of the disengaged state is a U-shaped function of the movement index.
outcomes.source: Figure 3F legend
outcomes.quote: There is a marked U-shaped relationship between both pupil diameter and movement index and the probability of being in the disengaged state
outcomes.notes: The mean P(disengaged) over 34 movement-index bins with at least 7 mice has a positive quadratic term (0.0225) with its vertex at 0.08, inside -4.25 to 4.0.

outcomes.statement: The movement index is equally correlated with face motion energy and with locomotion speed, and highly correlated with both in each mouse.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 4; Figure S5B and S5C
outcomes.quote: we combined these two measures into a single continuous measure of uninstructed movement levels termed the “movement index,” which is equally correlated with each measure
outcomes.notes: The two correlations agree to better than 0.0001 in every mouse (as they must by construction), with r from 0.674 to 0.855; reading (b), above 0.5, holds, and reading (a), above 0.7, fails in BW071 (0.674).

outcomes.statement: The absolute difference from the optimal pupil diameter is smaller in the optimal state (7%) than in the disengaged (12.6%) and sub-optimal (9%) states.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: These correlations translate to a significant decrease in the absolute difference from the calculated optimal pupil diameter during optimal state occupancy as compared to sub-optimal or disengaged states (optimal: 7% ± 0.3%, disengaged: 12.6% ± 1%, sub-optimal: 9% ± 0.5%
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) of O3 the absolute distance is 8.8% +/- 1.0% in the optimal state, 16.0% in the disengaged and 11.8% in the sub-optimal states, lower in the optimal state than in the disengaged (13 of 13, p = 0.00024) and sub-optimal states (13 of 13, p = 0.00024); reading (b) gives 8.8, 15.8 and 11.5 (p = 0.00024 and 0.0012). The order and the tests hold; all three values are larger than the paper's 7, 12.6 and 9.
deviations: Rests on the optimal pupils of fig3c-inverted-u-pupil, from this attempt's state fits.

outcomes.statement: Raw face motion energy tends to be larger in the optimal state (0.48 a.u.) than in the disengaged (0.43) and sub-optimal (0.44) states.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: a trend toward larger raw face motion energy during optimal state occupancy (optimal: 0.48 ± 0.02 a.u., disengaged: 0.43 ± 0.3 a.u., sub-optimal: 0.44 ± 0.03 a.u.; opt. vs. dis. p = 0.06, opt. vs. sub. p = 0.04
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) of O3 gives 0.482, 0.441 and 0.448 a.u., all within tolerance; optimal is the largest, above sub-optimal with p = 0.017 and above disengaged with p = 0.19 (paper 0.06). Reading (b) gives 0.485, 0.435 and 0.453 (p = 0.048 and 0.08).

outcomes.statement: Raw locomotion speed does not differ between optimal, disengaged and sub-optimal states (0.14 m/s in each).
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: but no significant differences in raw locomotion speed (optimal: 0.14 ± 0.02 m/s, disengaged: 0.14 ± 0.2 m/s, suboptimal: 0.14 ± 0.02 m/s; opt. vs. dis. p = 0.84, opt. vs. sub. p = 1
outcomes.notes: Optimal 0.136, disengaged 0.137, sub-optimal 0.136 m/s under reading (a), differences of at most 0.002 m/s, p = 0.84 and 0.89; reading (b) 0.137, 0.132 and 0.139 m/s, p = 0.68 and 0.95. Speeds are read as m/s although the file labels them cm/s (findings).

outcomes.statement: The 10-trial variability of pupil diameter, face motion energy and locomotion speed is lower in the optimal state than in the disengaged and sub-optimal states.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 6; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: For all arousal measures recorded−pupil diameter, face motion energy, and locomotion speed−we found significantly reduced variability during optimal performance state occupancy as compared to sub-optimal or disengaged states

statistics.about: pupil, optimal against disengaged (stars drawn by Figure4.py)
face motion energy, optimal against disengaged
face motion energy, optimal against sub-optimal

outcomes.notes: All six differences have the stated sign. Pupil, optimal against disengaged p = 0.00024 and against sub-optimal p = 0.0012; face p = 0.0024 and 0.017; locomotion p = 0.0012 and 0.057. Five of six tests pass.

outcomes.statement: Variability of the measures decreases on entering the optimal state and increases on leaving it.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 6; Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: Strikingly, this decrease in variability predicts transitions into and out of the optimal state

Of the four comparisons the figure marks, pupil exit (p = 0.0012), locomotion entry (p = 0.04) and locomotion exit (p = 0.0012) pass, face entry (p = 0.11) does not. 9 to 85 entries and 18 to 125 exits per mouse.

outcomes.statement: The correlation between pupil diameter and the movement index is lower during the optimal state than during the disengaged and sub-optimal states.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 7; Figures 4C and 4D
outcomes.quote: During optimal state epochs, the correlation between pupil diameter and the movement index is significantly reduced across subjects

statistics.about: optimal against disengaged (stars drawn by Figure4.py)

outcomes.notes: Mean r 0.077 (optimal), 0.439 (disengaged), 0.267 (sub-optimal); optimal lower than disengaged in 13 of 13 (p = 0.00024) and than sub-optimal in 12 of 13 (p = 0.00049). Disengaged is higher than sub-optimal (p = 0.0081), as the figure marks.

outcomes.statement: The correlations of pupil diameter with face motion energy and with locomotion speed are also reduced during the optimal state.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal and uninstructed movement, paragraph 7; Figure S6B and S6D
outcomes.quote: This decrease in correlation is also seen when considering individual measures of face motion energy and locomotion speed

statistics.about: pupil and face motion energy correlation, optimal against other states

outcomes.notes: Pupil with face, optimal lower than disengaged (p = 0.0024) and sub-optimal (p = 0.00049). Pupil with locomotion, lower than disengaged (p = 0.0017), not significantly lower than sub-optimal (p = 0.068). The face with locomotion correlation is also lower in the optimal state (p = 0.00049 and 0.01).

outcomes.statement: The inter-trial interval is long enough that trial-evoked responses do not carry over; correlations of the measures at trial start with the prior ITI are weak and centered on zero, and evoked pupil responses do not differ across performance states.
outcomes.source: Figure S1C and S1D
outcomes.quote: Correlations between all measures at the start of a trial and prior inter trial intervals are weak and centered around zero across mice. (D) Average evoked pupil responses of mice are not significantly different across performance states

statistics.about: evoked pupil response across performance states

outcomes.notes: Median r with the preceding ITI, pupil -0.044, locomotion -0.007, face -0.044, none different from zero (p = 0.13, 0.89, 0.27), so the ITI part holds under readings (a) and (b). The Kruskal-Wallis test of the per-mouse median evoked pupil response over the four groups gives H = 4.38, p = 0.22 (three discrete states, p = 0.15); group means -1.19, 1.57, 0.2 and -0.51% of the maximum.

outcomes.statement: In linear regressions of state probability on the measures, the quadratic weights of pupil diameter and of locomotion speed are negative for the optimal state and positive for the disengaged state, as are the weights of their 10-trial SDs, while face motion energy weights center on zero.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 3; Figure S8A
outcomes.quote: weights for the quadratic terms fit to predict optimal state probability were negative for pupil diameter across mice ... and the weights were positive when fit to disengaged state probabilities ... This was also true for quadratic terms of locomotion speed, while face motion energy had weights centered around zero across subjects
outcomes.notes: Optimal fits, pupil squared, locomotion squared, pupil SD and locomotion SD weights negative (medians -1.11, -1.10, -0.26, -0.33; Wilcoxon against zero p = 0.00024, 0.0012, 0.0081, 0.027). Disengaged fits, the same weights positive (0.56, 0.64, 0.19, 0.20; p = 0.00049, 0.00024, 0.033, 0.0081). Face squared and face SD weights do not differ from zero (p 0.19 to 0.84). Reading (a) holds, and so does (b).

outcomes.statement: With the movement index, the quadratic movement weight is negative for the optimal state, and the pupil-by-movement interaction is the only consistent weight for sub-optimal states (0.42 +/- 0.11), differing from its weight for the optimal state (-0.95 +/- 0.21).
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 3; Figure S8B
outcomes.quote: the only consistently weighted feature across fits to sub-optimal state probabilities was the interaction between pupil diameter and the movement index ( Figure S8B ; 0.42 ± 0.11), which was also significantly different than weights fit to optimal state probability (−0.95 ± 0.21

statistics.n: sub-optimal state fits against 13 optimal state fits

outcomes.notes: Pupil-by-movement weight 0.41 +/- 0.10 over 21 sub-optimal fits and -0.95 +/- 0.21 over 13 optimal fits, rank-sum p = 3.8e-06; quadratic movement weight of the optimal fits -1.30. Among the sub-optimal weights only the interaction differs from zero (p below 0.001).

outcomes.statement: For every mouse, support vector machines on the value and 10-trial variability of the measures predict the performance state above chance, with 88.2% +/- 1.8% accuracy for optimal against disengaged and 77.7% +/- 2% for optimal against sub-optimal states.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 1; Figures 5B and 5C
outcomes.quote: We found that for all subjects, performance states could be significantly predicted using the recorded arousal measures with high accuracy (opt. vs. dis. = 88.2% ± 1.8%; opt. vs. sub. = 77.7% ± 2%
outcomes.notes: Eight features unshuffled (condition 13), 88.9% +/- 1.7% over 13 optimal against disengaged classifications and 78.4% +/- 1.8% over 20 optimal against sub-optimal classifications; the "All measures" condition 0 gives 88.5% and 77.7%. All 33 classifications are significant under readings (a), (b) and (c). The paper has 19 sub-optimal classifications; this attempt's fits give 21 sub-optimal states, 20 with enough trials.
deviations: 3 runs per shuffled condition and 20 null runs, in place of 1000, to fit the time limit. The unshuffled condition does not vary between runs. With 20 null runs the null SD and its 95th percentile are estimated less precisely.
Rests on this attempt's state fits (figs2-n-states).

outcomes.statement: Pupil diameter (value and variability) is the best single raw measure for state classification, better than face motion energy and only slightly better than locomotion speed.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 2; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: Pupil diameter (value and trial-to-trial variability) was the best individual raw measure for state classification

statistics.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over optimal state classifications

The z-scores and reading (b) agree for face (p from 0.00029 to 0.0013); under (b) pupil is also above locomotion (p = 0.029 and 0.022).

outcomes.statement: The movement index is the best predictor of performance state, encoding more information about states than pupil diameter.
outcomes.source: Results, Arousal measures predict optimal performance state, paragraph 2; Figure 5C
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, we found that the best predictor of performance state was the computed movement index incorporating face motion energy and locomotion speed, which encoded more information about states compared to pupil diameter

The movement index is not better than pupil. The code's conditions shown as variants give higher accuracy for the movement-index classifier, condition 5 (movement index kept with the pupil value) 75.7% (p = 1.3e-05) and condition 1 (face and locomotion shuffled) 77.9% (p = 2.3e-10), but both keep pupil information, so they compare pupil and movement together against pupil alone and do not test the claim.

findings.statement: The running_speed series of every file is labelled cm/s, but its values (session medians around 0.07, 99th percentiles up to 0.67) are in m/s, the unit of the paper and of its code.

The dandiset holds 391 stage 5 and 6 sessions of the 13 included mice, where the paper analysed 381. The paper's inclusion criteria select 376 of them counted from the reward series and 375 counted from the hits, and nothing in the dandiset marks which sessions the paper used.

The training sessions before stage 5, the other stage 5 and 6 sessions of the 500 the paper names, and the 18 mice that did not meet the inclusion criteria are not in the dandiset, so the training duration (21 +/- 8 sessions) cannot be tested.
In 38 of the 391 sessions the post hoc pupil diameter series is present but entirely missing values (14 of BW046's 34 sessions), so those sessions have no pupil measure.
The rig names in the session metadata are spelled several ways for what appear to be the same rigs (Box 1, Box1, Boox1).

Question for the paper's authors. Figure2.py types each state by its nearest template with nansum, so a state with no trial of posterior 0.8 or more in the sessions where the optimal state occurs scores 0 against every template and displaces the optimal label. In this attempt's fits one state of BW059 is such a state; it was typed on all sessions. How were such states handled, and which 381 sessions were analysed?

entries.name: 000678-hulsey-2024
entries.title: Arousal, uninstructed movements and decision-making states in mice (Hulsey et al. 2024)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Hulsey, Zumwalt, Mazzucato, McCormick and Jaramillo (2024) on dandiset 000678, which holds the stage 5 and 6 behavioral sessions of 13 mice performing auditory or visual discrimination, with pupil diameter, face motion energy and locomotion speed. It fits the paper's GLM-HMM to each mouse's choices, labels the performance states, and relates the states to the arousal and movement measures, including the support vector machine decoding of the states.
